---
title: "Bayesian linear regression"
---

The earlier Bayesian chapters introduced [posterior distributions](../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd) and [prior predictive distributions](../statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions.qmd). Their [draw-wise treatment of contrasts](../statistical-inference/posterior-summaries.qmd#preserving-joint-uncertainty-in-a-contrast) will matter once predictions combine several coefficients. We now apply those ideas to the same ordinary linear regression likelihood used for [frequentist fitting](frequentist-linear-regression.qmd).

The ordinary linear regression model is

$$
Y_i\mid x_i,\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2).
$$

Frequentist fitting treated $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, and $\sigma$ as fixed unknown parameters. [**Bayesian linear regression**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html) adds prior distributions for them.

The conditional response model has not changed. The new step is to represent
uncertainty about the coefficients and conditional standard deviation before observing the
responses. Instead of
starting with one unknown line, the model starts with a distribution over lines.

## Assigning a prior to each coefficient

Suppose the response is log reading time and surprisal has been centered at 5 bits. One possible specification is

$$
\beta_0\sim\mathcal{N}(6,.25^2)
$$

and


$$
\beta_1\sim\mathcal{N}(0,.10^2).
$$

The intercept prior places most prior density on expected log reading times near 6 at the reference surprisal.

Since surprisal was centered at 5 bits, $\beta_0$ is the expected log reading
time at 5 bits. The prior is thus attached to a specific linguistic reference point.
If we had not centered the predictor, the same numerical prior would describe
expected log reading time at 0 bits, which may be outside the observed range.

The slope prior is centered at no association and represents most plausible changes per bit as modest on the log-time scale.

About 95 percent of a normal distribution lies within roughly two standard
deviations of its mean. Thus this prior places about 95 percent of its mass
between $-.20$ and $.20$ log-time units per bit. Across a four-bit surprisal
contrast, those endpoints imply conditional-mean changes of $-.80$ and $.80$.
The four-bit implication is often easier to assess than a one-bit coefficient.

The conditional standard deviation also needs a prior that assigns probability only to positive values:

$$
\sigma\sim p_+(\sigma).
$$

For current purposes, suppose $p_+$ is a half-normal distribution with scale
$.25$:

$$
\sigma\sim\operatorname{Normal}^+(0,.25^2).
$$

The superscript $+$ means that negative draws are excluded. This prior assigns
its greatest density near zero while allowing progressively less density for
larger response variation.

## Priors inherit measurement units

A prior standard deviation of $.10$ for a log-time slope is not automatically suitable for a raw-millisecond slope. The coefficient's units combine response units per predictor unit.

Centering changes the intercept's reference point, and rescaling a predictor changes the numerical slope. Prior choices must be interpreted after those transformations are declared.

Suppose we replace surprisal in bits, $x$, with half-bit units,

$$
x^*=2x.
$$

A one-unit increase in $x^*$ is only a half-bit increase. To represent the same
line, the new slope must be

$$
\beta_1^*=\frac{\beta_1}{2}.
$$

The prior standard deviation must likewise change from $.10$ to $.05$ if the
prior is meant to represent the same response-scale changes. Copying a numerical
prior across predictor units would change the model.

## Inspecting prior predictions

Draw parameter values from the priors, calculate conditional means across the observed surprisal range, and draw possible reading times:

$$
\widetilde{Y}_i
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2).
$$

If the prior model routinely predicts impossible or implausible reading times, the coefficient priors need revision. Prior predictive checking is more informative than calling a normal prior “weak” without examining its response-scale implications.

We can sample prior conditional means without fitting the data:

```{r}
#| label: draw-prior-regression-lines
#| echo: true
set.seed(214)

n_draws <- 1000
beta_0 <- rnorm(n_draws, mean = 6, sd = .25)
beta_1 <- rnorm(n_draws, mean = 0, sd = .10)
sigma <- abs(rnorm(n_draws, mean = 0, sd = .25))

centered_surprisal <- c(-3, 0, 4)

prior_means <- sapply(
  centered_surprisal,
  function(x) beta_0 + beta_1 * x
)

apply(prior_means, 2, quantile, probs = c(.025, .5, .975))
```

The three columns summarize prior expected log reading times at 2, 5, and 9
bits on the original scale. The intervals widen away from the centered reference
because uncertainty about the slope contributes more strongly at larger
distances from zero.

To inspect possible observations rather than conditional means, we would also
draw residual variation using `sigma`. This produces a wider distribution because
individual responses vary around each sampled line.

## Updating to a posterior

Bayes' rule combines the prior model and normal likelihood:

$$
p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma\mid\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})
\propto
p(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x},\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma)
p(\beta_0)p(\beta_1)p(\sigma).
$$

Posterior draws represent joint uncertainty in the line and conditional standard deviation.

The word *joint* is load-bearing. A posterior draw contains one compatible value
of the intercept, slope, and conditional standard deviation. Combining an intercept from one draw
with a slope from another would break the dependencies learned from the data.

For posterior draw $s$, the conditional mean at predictor value $x$ is

$$
m^{(s)}(x)
=\beta_0^{(s)}+\beta_1^{(s)}x.
$$

Repeating this calculation across draws gives a posterior distribution over the
conditional mean at that predictor value.

A 95% credible interval for $\beta_1$ contains 95% of that coefficient's posterior probability. This is a posterior statement, not the repeated-sampling statement attached to a confidence interval.

## Interpreting a posterior contrast

Suppose we want the conditional-mean difference between 3 and 7 bits. In centered
units these values are $-2$ and $2$. For every posterior draw,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta^{(s)}
&=m^{(s)}(2)-m^{(s)}(-2)\\
&=4\beta_1^{(s)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The posterior distribution of $4\beta_1$ directly represents uncertainty about
the four-bit contrast. This derived quantity preserves joint posterior
uncertainty because it is calculated within each draw.

## Evaluating priors on the response scale

Terms such as *weakly informative* do not determine a prior independently of the
measurement scale and predictor range. A verbal label such as *weakly informative* does not by itself justify an unexamined numerical prior.

A normal slope prior with standard deviation 1 may be modest for one response
scale and extreme for another. The response-scale predictions decide. A distribution over regression lines is
useful precisely because it lets us inspect those predictions before the data
pull the model toward an observed line.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the scale"}
1. If surprisal is changed from bits to half-bit units, how does the numerical
   slope change? Why must the slope prior change with it?
2. What reference point does the displayed intercept prior describe?
3. Why must a posterior contrast be calculated within each joint draw?
4. Explain why a label such as *weakly informative* does not justify a numerical prior without a scale check.
:::
